chantedPrayers.text: Liberating Prayer O Blessed One, Shakyamuni Buddha, precious Treasury of Compassion, Bestower of Supreme Inner Peace. You who love all beings without exception are the source of happiness and goodness, and you guide us to the liberating path. Your body is a wish-fulfilling jewel, your speech is supreme, purifying nectar, and your mind is refuge for all living beings. With folded palms I turn to you, Supreme unchanging Friend. I request from the depths of my heart, please give me the light of your wisdom to dispel the darkness of my mind and to heal my mental continuum. Please nourish me with your goodness, that I in turn may nourish all beings with an unceasing banquet of delight. Through your compassionate intention, your blessings and virtuous deeds, and my strong wish to rely upon you, may all suffering quickly cease and all happiness and joy be fulfilled, and may holy Dharma flourish forevermore. Going for Refuge I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. Generating Bodhichitta Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Four Immeasurables May everyone be happy, May everyone be free from misery, May no one ever be separated from their happiness, May everyone have equanimity, free from hatred and attachment. Visualizing the Field for Accumulating Merit In the space before me is the living Buddha Shakyamuni, surrounded by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, like the full moon surrounded by stars. Prayer of Seven Limbs With my body, speech, and mind, humbly I prostrate, and make offerings both set out and imagined. I confess my wrong deeds from all time and rejoice in the virtues of all. Please stay until samsara ceases and turn the Wheel of Dharma for us. I dedicate all virtues to great enlightenment. Offering the Mandala The ground sprinkled with perfume and spread with flowers, The Great Mountain, four lands, sun and moon, Seen as a Buddha Land and offered thus, May all beings enjoy such Pure Lands. The objects that give rise to my attachment, hatred, and confusion, my friends, enemies, and strangers, our bodies and enjoyments â€” please accept these and bless me to be released directly from the three poisons. IDAM GURU RATNA MANDALAKAM NIRYATAYAMI. Prayer of the Stages of the Path The path begins with strong reliance On my kind Teacher, source of all good; O Bless me with this understanding To follow him with great devotion. This human life with all its freedoms, Exceedingly rare and most meaningful â€” O Bless me with this understanding All day and night to seize its essence. My body, like a water bubble, Decays and dies so very quickly; After death come results of karma, Just as the shadow of a body. With this firm knowledge and target of remembrance Bless me to be extremely cautious, Always avoiding harmful actions And gathering abundant virtue. Samsaraâ€™s pleasures are deceptive, Give no contentment, only torment; So please bless me to strive sincerely To gain the bliss of perfect freedom. O Bless me so that from this pure thought Come great unfailing conscientiousness, To keep as my essential practice The Dharmaâ€™s root, the Pratimoksha. Just like myself, all my kind mothers Are drowning in samsaraâ€™s ocean; O So that I may soon release them, Bless me to train in bodhichitta. But I cannot become a Buddha By this alone without three ethics; So bless me with the strength to practise The Bodhisattvaâ€™s ordination. By pacifying my distractions And analyzing perfect meanings, Bless me to quickly gain the union Of special insight and quiescence. When I become a pure container Through the karma path, bless me to enter The essence practice of good fortune, The supreme vehicle, the Tantra. The two attainments both depend on My sacred vows and my commitments; Bless me to understand this clearly And keep them at the cost of my life. By constant practice in four sessions, The way explained by holy Teachers, O Bless me to gain both the stages Which are the essence of the Tantras. May those who guide me on the good path And my companions all have long lives; Bless me to pacify completely All obstacles, outer and inner. May I always find perfect Teachers And take delight in holy Dharma, Accomplish all grounds and paths swiftly, And gain the state of Vajradhara. Receiving Blessings From the hearts of all the holy beings, streams of light and nectar flow down, granting blessings and purifying.

guidedMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
guidedMeditation.text:
We can remember that mental prostration means showing respect or feeling a mind of respect towards others, both to Buddhas and to living beings. Look at the last two weeks and check critically and clearly how your meditation break practice went of respecting others. We can ask ourselves, did I remember to do this? Did I remember each week? Did I remember each day? Did I remember each hour?

For example, over the last 24 hours, how often did we remember to actively practice respecting others? Really check this and see if we remembered and practiced or if we forgot. If we had a strong degree of mindfulness, we can really rejoice in this and explore what went well, what we did to make this happen. And if we forgot or had little mindfulness over these two weeks, we should ask ourselves, why is that? Did I not care? Was I distracted? Did I have things I was more interested in?

If we were very mindful, we rejoice and think, where will this lead me? How will this change my life? But if our mindfulness was weak, we can also ask, where will this lead me? What will be the results of this? In the last couple of minutes, just reach some singular conclusion to help us going forward in our life. And just hold that single-pointedly, deep in our heart. And then, in our own time, we can gradually arise from our practice.

postMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postMeditation.text: Does anyone want to be the lucky duck reader of Guide to the Bodhisattva's Way of Life? Okay. Oh, and yes, thank you. Let's say 24. And then we'll start dabbling with some of the incredible purification verses. 24 through — oh, it's so hard to stop. They get better and better and better, so it's like such a cliffhanger to have to stop at one of them. Okay, I'm just going to pull the band-aid off. 36. Okay. 24 to 36.

shantidevaReading.speaker: Ryan
shantidevaReading.text:
(24) To all the Buddhas abiding in the three times,
The Dharma and the Supreme Assembly,
I prostrate with as many emanated bodies
As there are atoms in all the worlds.

(25) I prostrate to the bases for generating bodhichitta,
To the images of Buddha’s body, speech and mind,
To the Abbots and Preceptors,
And to the supreme practitioners on the path.

(26) Until I attain the essence of great enlightenment,
I will go for refuge to the Buddhas;
Likewise, I will go for refuge to Dharma
And to the assembly of Bodhisattvas.

(27) With my palms pressed together, I make requests
To those endowed with great compassion —
The perfect Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas
Who abide throughout the ten directions.

(28) Since beginningless time in samsara,
Throughout this and all my previous lives,
Out of ignorance I have committed evil,
Ordered it to be committed,

(29) And, overwhelmed by deceptive ignorance,
Rejoiced in its being committed by others.
Seeing all these to be grave mistakes,
From the depths of my heart I confess them to the holy beings.

(30) Whatever harmful actions of body, speech or mind
I have done under the influence of delusion
Towards the Three Precious Jewels,
My father and mother, my Spiritual Guide, and others —

(31) All the extremely unbearable evil actions
Committed by me, an evil person
Polluted by many faults —
I confess before the Deliverers, the enlightened beings.

(32) But I might die before I purify
All my negativities;
O please protect me so that I
May surely and swiftly be freed from them.

(33) Since the untrustworthy Lord of Death
Will not wait while I purify my evils,
Regardless of whether I am sick or not,
This momentary life is unreliable.

(34) I shall have to leave everything and depart alone
But, through failing to understand this,
I have committed many kinds of evil action
With respect to my friends and others.

(35) And yet my friends will become nothing
And others will also become nothing.
Even I shall become nothing;
Likewise, everything will become nothing.

(36) Just like an experience in a dream,
Everything I now enjoy
Will become a mere recollection,
For what has passed cannot be seen again.

postReading.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postReading.text:
These are actually very famous, and people traditionally will memorize these verses as a core practice — the confession verses that we got into after a couple of verses. And I believe when ordained people do their ritual for retaking their vows, they often will recite these exact verses because they're so famous and powerful. And Shantideva is a supreme monk, an example.

Okay, so then — we were respecting others, prostrating to others, and doing whatever else we were getting up to in our meditation break practice. I'd love to hear how that went and/or didn't go.

practiceReports.speaker: Ryan
practiceReports.text:
I'm not quite up to seeing everyone as a Buddha yet, but I found a way in that really helped work for me. What is the one thing everyone's an expert on? Themselves. So whenever people were talking, I'm like, I'm learning about them and their thoughts and their feelings, and they're telling me who they are. And I really can say that I don't know anything about these people. So I could learn a lot just by listening to them share whatever they were saying.

And then sort of making it into an emptiness practice, it was helpful to realize that they were all creations of my mind. So in a way, whenever they were reporting to me, even if it sounded deluded, I was actually only kind of hearing secondhand about my own delusions. If I didn't have delusions in my mind, I wouldn't be seeing and hearing these people report these things to me. So I learned a lot.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Sounds great. Well done. Thank you very much. Suzanne, yes.

practiceReports.speaker: Suzanne
practiceReports.text:
I haven't shared in a while because everything was going fine. I do my practice steadily. Nothing, no great insights or anything, but nothing bad either. Just slow and steady, fine. Until the Festival. And I think I'm broken now. I haven't been able to do my practice. I've also been very sick. I don't know if I'm in a crash or I'm actually sick.

But I can't seem to do my Heart Jewel. I was doing basically Heart Jewel and my mantras. I did some mantras. But I can't seem to get back to it. It's like I overheard the Liberating Prayer or something. I just feel really, really burnt out. And also people have been really on my nerves lately. And I'm thinking I'm not respecting them, number one. And number two, I'm going to need to do some purification. So hopefully this little burnout thing will end soon because I really think I need to purify.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Yeah. What do you think is the cause of the burnout? Festival is not the cause, okay? Festival is the cause of enlightenment. It cannot be a cause of burnout. So that's not an answer. So what's the cause?

practiceReports.speaker: Suzanne
practiceReports.text: Why is this too much for me? I just pushed myself too much?

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Yeah, there we go. That's more clear. We have to be really clear that Festival is not the cause of burnout. Festival is the cause of enlightenment. That's its only effect. So if we have some kind of negative side effect, it's something coming from within, our own mind. It was going too far or pushing too much or going beyond our capacity. It's good to notice that and learn about ourselves. What can I do? What can I not do? Where am I at in my life? Why do I go too far sometimes?

As you noted, there's definitely a big purification thing there. If we use a lot of the opponents and take a lot of steps and something doesn't seem to be changing, it's often just a sign of a negative karma thing. In which case, the answer is to uproot some of this negative karma and purify. So there's the cognitive exploration — psychologically, why do I go too far? And then if we're taking the right steps and doing the right practices and there's still this symptom, at some point we have to conclude this is just some negative karma that I have to look at. That's where my energy needs to go. Thank you, Suzanne.

practiceReports.speaker: Anne P
practiceReports.text:
So what happened recently was I moved back to Pennsylvania. And although I've lived there off and on for 20 years and had a job there once for six years, this time when I moved back, as soon as I got there, I felt like I was in the Pure Land. What happened was that just before I moved, I had the fire ceremony, Vajradaka, and I was giving away identification as a landlord. I got a lot of information about how this landlord thing dated back to 1970 when I moved to New York City.

So then I get to Chester County, and I'm giving away being a landlord, giving away being a landlord. And I get there, and it's like, I can't believe it — it's like the Pure Land. And I'm a bodhisattva. So it's been very pleasant. I really like it. I think it's a great thing. Screw the landlord stuff.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Right, so you changed the label from landlord to bodhisattva. Anyone who could see Pennsylvania as the Pure Land is very highly realized. Thank you very much. It's beautiful. And I'm glad that Vajradaka and purification helped facilitate that shift. Dale, yes, thank you. And then Ryan after that. And then Adriana after that.

practiceReports.speaker: Dale
practiceReports.text:
So I was at the Festival, which I thought was wonderful. But during the empowerment, I did not feel much of anything. And that's unusual because I normally do. However, two things. When I got home, I started to feel differently. I felt more peaceful. I felt the blessings. I was walking down the street and all of a sudden I said, oh, this could be Heruka's Pure Land. I don't have to see this with the scaffolding and the noise and the traffic. And I have never done that before — just visualize myself in Heruka's Pure Land. Other thoughts were coming up that were normally not like me, but very loving and very open and giving.

Plus, I decided to watch less TV, which is a huge deal for me because that would be my evening, and I'm using that time to read and to learn. The second thing that happened is I realized there are two people currently in my life who I have to really invoke patience because they drive me nuts. And I was pushing them away and not wanting to deal with it, but I realized — use these two people as a learning experience about yourself. So that's what I got out of it.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Thank you, Dale. It's lovely. And it's a good reminder that an empowerment plants a seed, a karmic seed in our mind to attain realizations. And then the teachings of the Festival are a blessing transmission of the oral lineage — Buddha's speech getting transmitted to us. So sometimes we don't feel anything because karmic seeds don't ripen instantly. It's a very rapid effect compared to what normally could happen, a few months, a few years.

It's an important skill when we receive an empowerment to try not to push for a feeling, because it can take away from the experience. What we should instead be thinking is, I'm so happy I'm planting these incredible seeds in my mind to gain realizations. If our mind is pushing for a feeling for the whole event, it can become quite unhappy, and that's not based in wisdom. We just think, I'm creating the cause. I'm getting the seed for enlightenment here. Thanks so much. Ryan, yes, thank you.

practiceReports.speaker: Ryan
practiceReports.text:
I'll share one of the takeaways from the U.S. Festival. This was not in the classroom — this was outside the temple. We were out in the parking lot every day, me, Jose, Mary Ann, and others. And we were there to love people and guide people. After being there three, four days, you get to know the people. And I started having conversations with people, especially resident teachers or monks or nuns.

I remember one conversation with one nun in the car. She had this big smile on her face. And I asked her, I'm going back after the Festival to Brooklyn and I have to love people — how do I get that love? And she said, remember this: I do, I do, I do. I do love, I love people. I do, I do, I do. And she was doing this beautiful mudra from the car.

The two takeaways: first, when I come back to Brooklyn, it's like, who says I don't love people? I do love people. And I remembered this morning — I do, I do, I do — on the train. Second, the most important thing about why it's important to go to Festivals is that you get to see and have conversations with people — laypeople, ordained family, resident teachers — that you usually don't see. You can get teachings on the go, even in the parking lot, even on the lines to the coffee.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Thank you, Ryan. The practice you're describing is thinking, I do love people. It's actually an important thought. Basically, I'm a loving person. Sometimes we try to develop love and compassion on the basis of thinking, I'm not a loving person, I'm not a compassionate person. But we shouldn't think like that. We should think, I am a loving person.

And you're right, that is definitely one of the functions of going to an event like that — surrounded by a bunch of incredible yogis. Where do you find them? The people we talk to at work, we see around the street — they have no idea what's going on. They don't understand emptiness. They don't have a tantric practice. There's not that many people in the country who are doing that. So to get them all in one place, where you can mine them for everything they've got, and they're just delighted to share, is an incredibly lucky opportunity. Thanks, Ryan. Adriana, thank you.

practiceReports.speaker: Adriana
practiceReports.text:
So I had the very special opportunity this week to be in a room with about 75 people who were so angry and hateful and just wanted to take me down, along with four of my colleagues. I did so much preparation, and the thing that helped me the most was I memorized this passage on page 66: “All my lifetimes I will offer all my bodies to the Buddhas and their sons. Please accept me, oh supreme heroes, as I reverently become your subject and follow your advice. Protected by your power, I will remain unafraid of samsara's sufferings, and I will benefit others. My previous evils will be purified, and in the future I will commit no more.”

I said that like hundreds of times, all day, for the whole week, preparing for this thing. And I have to tell you, I was so happy. Actually, it was the best experience I ever had. My colleagues were not so happy — they were offended and annoyed, and I saw them getting upset. And I was like, I'm so happy right now. When the students laughed at me, they mocked me — I was like, okay, today you are mocking me, and in the future may I teach you pure Buddha Dharma.

I left the meeting and I was so happy. I really don't like it when every year people try to fire me. And this year it's a petition with 776 signatures. It got so big. But I can do it. It's no problem. I just have to follow Buddha's advice. I feel like I had an experience where I don't have to be afraid.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Thank you, Adriana. It's a nice example of using the Dharma words to solve the problem. Buddha's speech is blessed — it's basically Buddha's mind appearing as speech. So memorizing a verse or passage and then using it and wielding it actively is a very powerful practice. It's much more powerful than us thinking through something in our own way. It's like a huge blazing rocket ship compared to a little skateboard. Because we're calling on Buddha's mind when we memorize Buddha's speech and recite it with faith. We're accessing a Buddha's mind, versus just trying to think through our problems in our normal way.

I'm not surprised that because you chose that specific method, it was a very moving experience. A normal thinky, analytical solution probably wouldn't have done much at all. It was actually going to your faith and connecting to Buddha's mind. That's what made a shift. Thank you very much. Mimi, yes, thanks, and then David after that.

practiceReports.speaker: Mimi
practiceReports.text:
So for the past two weeks, I have been pretty mindful about my practice, seeing myself as the lowest of them all. And so this is what happened. Last week, a patient came to the clinic, and he came in shackles. My team was pretty concerned and they were like, Mimi, can you see this patient? My first reaction was, I understand, it's something not common to see. It's okay, we'll just concentrate on his diabetes.

I was completely impartial until I actually went into the room and saw him. He was with three escorts, and he was so young — 17 and so beautiful. Light brown skin and green hazel eyes. I kept looking at him thinking, how can this young boy be incarcerated like this? And then I thought of my own son, who was also incarcerated at the same age and who I had seen come out in a jumpsuit and shackled in a similar fashion. This boy could be my son, could be Sebastian. I started getting a little traumatized.

But something happened in my mind. I think it was a blessing. I said, this boy is me. This boy is me. And those three escorts are my delusions. So I'm shackled and imprisoned in samsara by these three escorts: attachment, anger, ignorance. And I said to the boy, you know, now you have an opportunity to choose another path. But then I said them to myself — Mimi, you can also choose another path and get out of samsara.

When he left, I said to the escorts, I don't want him in the waiting room. I need you to escort him out. I don't want him humiliated. I don't want other patients to see him. They took him out through the back. I've been thinking about him — he's so present in my mind. He was an emanation. He's Tara.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Thank you, Mimi. It's a nice example of using one of the most supremely useful forms of respecting others — exchanging self with others, imputing I on all living beings, or “me.” Once you do that, there are all these magical things that happen. Especially using whatever is going on as a reflection of our own mind to help us understand what's going on inside ourselves, instead of viewing someone as an other, which can just put them in a box. And then all these little blessings and insights come through. Thank you for practicing that. David, last one, and then we'll get moving.

practiceReports.speaker: David
practiceReports.text:
So in the first week, I found it much easier to remember respecting others. I had family visiting, and there were a couple little incidents. One of my parents had an issue with one of their feet — a toenail situation. We got home, and I got out the nail file and just got to work on their toenail, something I would never ever have dreamed of doing. But it was actually really enjoyable. I could tell it meant a lot to them. When I think about that, I just get so happy — really on my knees, scraping that toenail.

One other thing, my brother was cold one time and I gave him my sweatshirt, and he was so happy with the sweatshirt. When I remember those things, it really makes me happy. I feel like I can rejoice in the virtue of that.

Week two, I mostly forgot about the whole practice, and I think it's because I didn't have a plan to remember. I do the six sessions, but I feel like I want to link the six sessions to my Lamrim practice and to TTP. Like some sort of system, because the first week I just happened to remember and the next week I just happened to forget. Week two I found myself getting annoyed a lot more, coincidentally. And then maybe a little similar to Adriana's words, I just kept repeating, anger is poison, anger is poison, over and over. Because when I'm actually getting annoyed, it doesn't seem like poison — it seems like right. It actually feels good in a weird way. So it was a bit of a battle week two, but that phrase helped me.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Yeah, thanks, David. It's great. Let's have a plan with our meditation break practice. Thank you very much.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
Okay, now we are on to Refuge, page 76, Meaningful to Behold.

“The third preliminary practice for purifying negativities and accumulating merit is to turn the mind to the proper and ultimate source of refuge. As Shantideva says: From this moment on, until I attain the essence of great enlightenment, I will go for refuge to the Buddhas, the Dharma, and the Supreme Assembly of Superior Bodhisattvas.”

“The explanation of going for refuge has five parts: the causes of going for refuge, the objects of going for refuge, the measurement of going for refuge perfectly, the commitments of going for refuge, the benefits of going for refuge.”

“If the causes of going for refuge are unknown to us, we will have no motivation to begin this practice. And if we do not know what the proper objects of refuge are, then to whom will we turn? If we do not know the measurement of going for refuge perfectly, we will not know how to complete this practice. And if we remain ignorant of the commitments of going for refuge, we will be unable to fulfill the purpose of this practice. Finally, if we do not know the benefits of going for refuge, we will deprive ourselves of the inspiration necessary for undertaking this practice sincerely and repeatedly.”

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
“Going for refuge is a major foundation of the Buddhist path. It signifies our determination to turn away from the endless cycle of confusion and dissatisfaction that has marked our life, and towards a saner, more wholesome way of living.” Those are beautiful little sentences. A saner, more wholesome way of living — that's the life of going for refuge. The life of not going for refuge is an endless cycle of confusion and dissatisfaction. Yeah, that's about right.

“As stated before, our past collection of negative actions of body, speech and mind has been responsible both for our day-to-day confusion and unhappiness and for our difficulty in gaining realizations along the spiritual path. If this uncontrolled pattern of behavior continues unchecked, it will lead us to even more acute states of suffering and torment in the future. Thus there are two interrelated causes for our taking refuge in Buddha, Dharma and Sangha. First, we must have a heartfelt dread of the miserable states of samsaric existence towards which our uncontrolled behavior is propelling us. In terms of Buddhist cosmology, this dread is interpreted as an intense aversion to the sufferings of the three lower realms, or further, as a feeling of being disgusted with the unsatisfactory nature of all states conditioned by ignorance.”

These words are fantastic. Dread, intense aversion, and disgusted. So when we think about samsara, do we feel disgust? Do we feel disgusted by our ordinary, contaminated aggregates? It's not with ourself — we're not our aggregates, we're not the delusions. Do we feel disgust towards the delusions? Dread is quite useful a word too. Do we have this sense of dread of the lower realms, or is it something abstract and not relevant to our normal life?

“In addition to this real dread, we must have an unshakable conviction and faith in the Three Jewels, understanding well how they have the power to protect us from all forms of suffering. Basing our conviction upon reason, proper authority, and most importantly our own experience, we turn to the Three Jewels of refuge with the thought that only they can show us the path away from fear and dissatisfaction and towards peace of mind.”

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
What do we think is the answer to the suffering of this world? What do we think? Where do we go for refuge as an answer? Geshe-la gives examples later about the police, or about doctors. We go for refuge to the police if we're fearful for our life. We go for refuge to a doctor if we're sick. Many people go for refuge to politics, and they think that's the answer — which is completely bizarre. It's just trying to fix samsara. It doesn't solve delusions. Police and doctors can't free us from ordinary death. They can't free us from rebirth. Politics can't do that. Entertainment definitely not — just fuels it further.

So we just check in our mind: what do I really think is the answer? What do I think about all day? What do I put my energy into as an answer? Really and honestly. When we're fearful, when we're unhappy, when we're worried — where do we go for relief? For refuge? For escape?

mainTeaching.speaker: David
mainTeaching.text:
I like that question. Because I think I do have a sense of clarity — these things are not the answer. But when we say “the answer,” I kind of mean the final answer. What popped into my head was this analogy: let's say I'm hiking and really tired. My final refuge is when I get back to my tent and lie down in my cot. But I've got to stop — it's miles away. So I need some temporary things, which are clearly to me not the final answer.

So when you said, what do you think about all day? I really do think the final refuge is spiritual practice. But I spend a lot of time thinking about temporary refuges. Because their effect will be felt more quickly. However, they have the shortcoming of not being an ultimate refuge. I spend all this time thinking about these temporary refuges.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
Yeah, like temporary reliefs. The heuristic that's pretty good is: if I need this temporary relief in order to get ultimate relief, then it makes sense. But if I'm distracting myself from ultimate relief, then it definitely doesn't make sense. If I'm deluding myself that it is the ultimate relief, it definitely doesn't make sense. And if it's purely superfluous and not necessary, then it doesn't make sense.

For example, getting a painkiller when you're in agony is not ultimate relief. But you need to be able to think, walk around, sleep at night. So you take that painkiller so that you can get ultimate relief — so you can use your mind for virtue and to realize emptiness. Once you have that relief, if you still take the painkiller, now that's an addiction. Getting rest so you can be clear-minded when awake — that's temporary relief you need. But sleeping the day away as an escape is just changing suffering.

I find that to be a useful heuristic. Am I doing this in order to get ultimate freedom? If so, fantastic. If not, maybe it's extra or distraction.

mainTeaching.speaker: Ryan
mainTeaching.text:
I feel it's tying together with your GP teachings. What am I paying attention to all day? Same with refuge — where am I looking for refuge? I was thinking, what am I paying attention to on a regular day? Most of my day I'm paying attention to comfort. Looking around for my next comfort. All this morning resisting Heart Jewel and Lamrim because I want to just be comfortable. Leave me alone. Let me chill on the couch, read a novel, have my next coffee.

Even when I come here, I come a few minutes earlier so I have time for a coffee. At the Starbucks in the train, I hope to get a seat. I'm collecting comfort around. That's my refuge. That's what I pay attention to throughout the day.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
Thanks, Ryan. It's a good point. Even a Dharma practice can be like this — in the name of just temporary comfort. Because it feels good. But it has nothing to do with future lives, liberation, enlightenment. It's just a sophisticated medication with very little side effects. That's not a spiritual path though — that's pleasure seeking, one of the worldly concerns.

We just notice that and we're aware. Let me start refining it. Let me really make my practice a spiritual path.

mainTeaching.speaker: David
mainTeaching.text: I have a question about using the spiritual path as just temporary relief. I think this question comes up from students around breathing meditation. Geshe-la says somewhere that breathing meditation can be very profound — we realize our problems don't exist outside our mind. If you do use it for temporary relief, is that temporary relief, or is it familiarizing your mind with inner peace? How do you tease those two things out?

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
It's just the intention mostly. If the intention is just to have happiness in the here and now, it doesn't create an effect of liberation. It's just about feeling good, so it's not really a spiritual path. It has to be on at least one of the three scopes: happiness in future lives, liberation from samsara, or Buddhahood. If you do a breathing meditation with the intention to benefit others or for any of those three scopes, then it's a spiritual path.

Where Geshe-la says it's a profound practice, it's that insight — that our happiness comes from within. Understanding that very deeply is very close to understanding emptiness. So there's wiggle room. But the point is about the intention. That's what makes something a spiritual path or not.

mainTeaching.speaker: David
mainTeaching.text: Brief follow-up. If your intention is to reduce your delusions, can that be spiritual even if you're not explicitly thinking about future lives?

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
“The Buddhist teachings describe three progressive levels of spiritual practice, and the dual causes for going for refuge described above vary according to which of these three levels we are on. A person at the initial level of motivation sees clearly how their mind is polluted by such violent delusions as hatred, jealousy, and greed. They fear that without proper training, this unruly mind will expose them to the intense suffering of the three lower realms. Such a person develops faith and conviction in the power of the Three Jewels to offer protection from this harm.”

“When a person progresses to the intermediate level of motivation, they see how the whole of samsaric existence is pervaded by dissatisfaction and suffering. Fed up with circling through this unending round of existence, the person turns to the Three Jewels for a method to gain complete liberation.”

“At the highest level of motivation, the spiritual seeker is motivated by great compassion. They transcend individual selfish concerns to see that all other beings are also whirling around in the darkness of their ignorance, creating the causes for more and more suffering for themselves. With an intense wish to help these beings, each of whom they recognize as having been their mother in previous lives, they turn to the Three Jewels with the conviction that only they can lead them to enlightenment.”

This should point our mind directly at the Lamrim, because the Lamrim is designed to help us develop these three scopes. The initial scope is the first five meditations, the intermediate scope is the sixth meditation, and the great scope is the twenty-first meditation. We can see how necessary it is to practice the Lamrim, or else we're not really on a spiritual path, because we're not cultivating these higher aims.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
What I want us to focus on for the rest of today is faith, specifically. There is this incredible section in Modern Buddhism. For Buddhists, faith in Buddha Shakyamuni is their spiritual life. It is the root of all Dharma realizations.

If we have deep faith in Buddha, we will naturally develop the strong wish to practice his teachings. This wish will definitely imply effort in Dharma practice. With strong effort, we'll accomplish permanent liberation from the suffering of this life and countless future lives. The attainment of permanent liberation depends on effort, which depends on the strong wish to practice Dharma, which in turn depends on deep faith in Buddha.

Faith, aspiration, effort, liberation. Then liberation, effort, aspiration, faith. It's a tight link. Therefore, if we truly want to experience great benefit from our practice of Buddhism, we need to develop and maintain deep faith in Buddha.

In a sense, this first bit is about having faith in faith. We're admiring faith, believing in the power of faith, and wishing to develop our faith. Why? Because it's the root of all spiritual attainments. Each one of us can have that wish equally, because it's not until we're Buddha that we've perfected our faith.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
How do we develop and maintain this faith? First, we should know why we need to attain permanent liberation from suffering. It is not enough just to experience temporary liberation from a particular suffering. All living beings, including animals, experience temporary liberation. Animals experience temporary liberation from human suffering, and humans from animal suffering. At the moment we may be free from physical suffering and mental pain, but this is only temporary. In the cycle of samsara, no one has permanent liberation.

So to grow my faith, I need to repeatedly think how temporary liberation is not good enough. It's unsatisfactory in different ways. One way is it's deceptive — it kind of works, and can make us miss the point altogether. Oh, I don't need Dharma, everything is better now. Sometimes I consider what kind of temporary liberations could dupe me off my path. What kind of little Maras could sneak in. What if everything just started to be wonderful and easy, and well-respected, and all this free time and wealth — would I go, I don't need to practice anymore?

The second reason temporary liberation is not enough is that we die. If we're not permanently liberated, some mess starts up. No guarantee of a precious human life, no guarantee a spiritual path starts in that life. Lastly, temporary liberations don't give us the ability to help other people. We might feel good, but what about everyone else? There's something selfish and hedonistic about temporary liberation.

announcements.speaker: Kadam Kyle
announcements.text: I'm wearing a Walk for World Peace T-shirt from last year. May 17th — maybe after the empowerment, our second most important event at KMC Brooklyn. Please do come and bring a friend.

dedication.speaker: Kadam Kyle
dedication.text: Let's dedicate. Through the virtues we've collected, may all living beings find lasting peace of mind, enlightenment. We can make any personal prayers or dedications. See you in a bit.

chantedPrayers.text: Liberating Prayer O Blessed One, Shakyamuni Buddha, precious Treasury of Compassion, Bestower of Supreme Inner Peace. You who love all beings without exception are the source of happiness and goodness, and you guide us to the liberating path. Your body is a wish-fulfilling jewel, your speech is supreme, purifying nectar, and your mind is refuge for all living beings. With folded palms I turn to you, Supreme unchanging Friend. I request from the depths of my heart, please give me the light of your wisdom to dispel the darkness of my mind and to heal my mental continuum. Please nourish me with your goodness, that I in turn may nourish all beings with an unceasing banquet of delight. Through your compassionate intention, your blessings and virtuous deeds, and my strong wish to rely upon you, may all suffering quickly cease and all happiness and joy be fulfilled, and may holy Dharma flourish forevermore.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
We'll continue on this subject of increasing our faith. Practically we already have a few ideas about how to use this in daily life. One is to increase our effort by increasing our faith — with any practice, instead of hammering away at it, put our energy into increasing our faith in the practice, and let that naturally flow downhill into effort, which is a much gentler way to practice. The second way is to start to think that temporary liberation is not enough — catching ourselves seeking just temporary liberations, noticing when we go, ah, that's better.

“How can we accomplish this? Only by putting Buddhist teachings into practice. This is because only Buddhist teachings are the actual methods to abandon our self-grasping ignorance, the source of all our suffering.” If something doesn't oppose self-grasping ignorance, it doesn't lead to permanent liberation. It can at best lead to temporary liberation.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
“In his teaching called The King of Concentration Sutra, Buddha says: A magician creates various things, such as horses, elephants, and so forth. His creations do not actually exist. You should know all things in the same way.”

This is one of Buddha's most famous teachings, because it's so starkly clear. It's not metaphorical. His creations do not actually exist. You should know all things in the same way. Oh, okay, thank you, Buddha — very clear.

This is why Geshe-la teaches that things that we normally see do not exist at all. Same meaning. “This teaching alone has the power to permanently liberate all living beings from their suffering. Through practicing and realizing this teaching, we can permanently eradicate the root of all our suffering, our self-grasping ignorance. When this happens, we'll experience the supreme permanent peace of mind known as nirvana.”

“Through understanding this, we'll deeply appreciate the great kindness of Buddha to all living beings in giving profound methods to achieve permanent liberation. Even our mother does not have this compassion that wishes to liberate us from these sufferings. Only Buddha has this compassion for all living beings without exception. Buddha is actually liberating us by revealing the wisdom path that leads us to the ultimate goal of human life.”

“We should contemplate this point again and again until we develop deep faith in Buddha. This faith is the object of our meditation. We should transform our mind into faith in Buddha and maintain it single-pointedly for as long as possible.”

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
It's important to move away from ever thinking of faith as a byproduct or a passive thing. It's a mental factor — compassion, non-hatred, non-attachment, wisdom. It's a state of mind that we cultivate very purposely.

This is the main thing hopefully we can all bring with us this week. Can I maintain my faith when I go for a walk? When I'm in a conversation? When I watch television? In the doctor's office? Getting yelled at? Getting scary news? In an argument? Can I maintain my mind of faith in those moments? Can I remember it and hold it in my heart?

The center of this is really thinking: I have faith in Buddha because he's teaching me emptiness specifically. Buddha's kind in lots of ways. But specifically and above all, because he teaches me emptiness. In a sense, our faith is really faith in emptiness. Therefore, Buddha's awesome. But it's actually faith in emptiness. That's the only way to attain permanent liberation.

So part of what gives us faith in emptiness is really proving to ourselves: why, precisely, is realizing emptiness going to lead to permanent liberation? Why, without emptiness, is it impossible to attain permanent liberation?

teaching.speaker: Adriana
teaching.text: Without knowing ultimate truth, you don't understand the relationship between your mind and its appearances. Until you realize emptiness completely, you will always have mistaken appearance and be tethered to samsaric appearance rather than pure appearance. We still blame others and external factors for our problems. We don't have full control. We're still tethered to samsara by karmic shackles.

teaching.speaker: Dale
teaching.text: I immediately think that you need to get rid of your delusions to get anywhere. Even though you may make progress, unless you really get enlightened, they're going to keep coming back. I think that's the real poison — delusions.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Thanks, Dale. It's helpful to sometimes think, what would it be like to have no attachment? Precisely no attachment — no looking for happiness outside of ourselves. It's very hard to imagine that without basically imagining a realization of emptiness. If we still grasp at a self or things as inherently existent, how could we have absolutely no attachment? Even in the highest god realm of pure bliss, we'd still be going, I could have even more bliss, I want this to last longer. There'd still be these attachments and mental pain.

So the dependent relationship is: all suffering comes from delusions. You can't get rid of the delusions, especially attachment and aversion, without realizing emptiness.

teaching.speaker: Sumit
teaching.text: Jumping off Dale's point — the root delusion is self-grasping. In particular, we're grasping at our contaminated aggregates, which is where pervasive suffering arises. The only way to stop grasping at our contaminated aggregates is through emptiness — that's literally what that is. So that's the only solution to pervasive suffering. The other sufferings, as you pointed out, you could be a god and make things pretty nice. But pervasive suffering requires emptiness to alleviate.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Yeah. You're basically saying that as long as there's an I imputed on an ordinary body and mind, that in and of itself — no matter how good things might be — is a state of suffering, which is called pervasive suffering. Without stopping that, without stopping thinking I on an ordinary body and mind, we are in a state of suffering no matter how spiritual we are.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
From Joyful Path, the Dharma Jewel is defined as: a perfectly purified truth in the continuum of a superior being, which has any of the eight good qualities, such as inconceivable. The eight good qualities: inconceivable, non-dual, non-conceptual, pure, clear, the side of the antidote, that which frees from attachment, the two truths are the definition of Dharma.

The actual Dharma Jewel is the third and fourth of the Four Noble Truths: true cessations and true paths, attained through practicing Buddhist teachings. A true cessation is permanent because it is the emptiness of a mind that has attained complete abandonment of any obstruction to the power of a true path. It is not merely the final abandonment of any delusion — it is the emptiness of a mind that has attained such a cessation.

Why is a true cessation permanent? If liberation is caused, and caused things are functioning, then why can't liberation end? The answer: it is permanent because it is the emptiness of a mind that has attained complete abandonment.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
The Sangha Jewel is defined as a superior being who has any of the eight good qualities, such as realization and freedom. A superior being is someone who's realized emptiness directly by practicing the three higher trainings. Since we cannot see any actual Sangha Jewels, we should regard as Sangha Jewel anyone keeping the Pratimoksha vows purely, the Bodhisattva vows purely, or the Tantric vows purely — and anyone else who's helping others and showing a good example.

Buddha Jewel is defined as the ultimate source of refuge having eight good qualities, such as non-produced. Non-produced refers to the true cessations that are the abandonment of the two obstructions. Since these true cessations are permanent, they are called non-produced. Being free from all faults, Buddha accomplishes everything effortlessly because they are free from conceptual thought.

Over time what we want to do is understand the real nature of the Three Jewels. The Dharma Jewel of emptiness is our object of faith in Dharma. The Sangha Jewel, people who realize emptiness, is our faith in Sangha. Buddha is one with emptiness — that's why we have faith in Buddha. And Buddha teaches and reveals emptiness.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: “One of Buddha's main functions is to bestow mental peace upon each and every living being by giving blessings. By themselves, living beings are unable to cultivate a peaceful mind.” Anyone have an explanation of why that's the case?

teaching.speaker: Mary Ann
teaching.text: Contaminated aggregates make it impossible because they're seeing things that don't exist and making us agitated.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Okay, what if I said, but I can still develop love and then get a peaceful mind?

teaching.speaker: Mary Ann
teaching.text: But the consciousness will rise up again and disturb. The pureness will be destroyed very soon by the aggregates that are tying us to samsara and all its temptations and bummers.

teaching.speaker: Sumit
teaching.text: Is it that a blessing is basically a necessary condition for the fruition of positive karma? Good feelings and happiness are just positive karma ripening. Unless you have the necessary conditions to cause positive karma to ripen, it can't happen. And I think one of those conditions is blessings.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Yeah, that's closer to the exact reason. When we study how to understand the mind, one of the causes of a virtuous mind is a blessing. It's like how do you get a cloud? You need moisture and pressure and space. Without moisture, you just can't get a cloud. A blessing is actually a 100% required contributory cause for a virtuous mind. Which is something we should really ponder. Is it utterly impossible to cultivate a virtuous mind without a blessing?

teaching.speaker: David
teaching.text: What about just generating a lot of positive karma? If you have a bunch of virtuous actions, why wouldn't that be enough to get a peaceful mind?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Exactly! That's exactly the question. Why is that not enough? Why does there have to be a blessing from Buddha as part of the flow?

When Venerable Geshe-la taught on the union of two truths — the union of appearance and emptiness — he said, when we think that I am Heruka, one with emptiness, we should think: this is the real truth. I am correctly identifying myself now. Unmistaken appearance is this. It's only Buddha who is at one with the truth, with reality. That's the truth — a Buddha, not other than emptiness. Everything else is complete fiction and falsity.

When we're receiving a blessing, we're actually connecting with the truth. That's all a blessing is. And without connecting with the truth, we're not going to get a peaceful mind. We're completely out of touch with reality, grasping at the contaminated aggregates.

It has to do with relationship. The self on its own is a closed loop. It can't do anything on its own. It's completely self-referential, which is basically non-existent. You can't get a peaceful mind on your own. It always has to be in relationship to something else. The word blessing means to transform — for our mind to transform from an ego state to a positive state. It's implying that on its own, the mind can't transform from a negative state to a positive state. It needs another influence.

Practically, over these two weeks: how can we really bring our faith into our daily life, especially our faith in emptiness?

conclusion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
conclusion.text: Alright, everyone. Come one, come all. Practicing in the break — maintaining faith. Temporary liberations are not enough. Faith in emptiness. One of those things. Ben, yes?

conclusion.speaker: Ben
conclusion.text: We were talking about practicing by words and reminding ourselves of the reasons for our faith by thinking about the ways that we know that Buddha's teachings are leading us towards liberation, and interrupting. We talked about maybe having a list of reasons that you can use to interrupt your mind of non-faith when you experience it.

conclusion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
conclusion.text:
Love that, Ben. That's really beautiful and very practical. You have a list of reasons, and you said treating every activity by words — little quotes from the teachings, Buddha's words. You go through them when a mind of non-faith or doubt arises, reciting or remembering or recalling them.

It's like having words that we have faith in, teachings that we feel are infallible or true, and we can always go back to them. Using those exact words, those exact teachings, even going through a list — that's a very nice approach. Thank you. Anything else? Once, twice, sold. I think that's it. Have a lovely week. You can dedicate now.

closingPrayer.text: Prayer of the Virtuous Tradition So that the tradition of Je Tsongkhapa, the King of the Dharma, may flourish, may all obstacles be pacified and may all favorable conditions abound. Through the two collections of myself and others gathered throughout the three times, may the doctrine of Conqueror Losang Dragpa flourish forevermore.
